CVE-2026-12615.5ac475d2ab95ea95d2890c745a05e5275137fb98:
fix(security): isolate Stanford Java options and clean temp files (#3683)

Several Stanford/Java wrappers wrote plaintext user input to delete=False temporary files and removed those files only after Java execution succeeded. If Java raised, the temporary input files remained on disk.

The wrappers also configured request-specific Java options by mutating the process-global nltk.internals._java_options. Failures or concurrent requests could leave wrapper-specific Java flags visible to later Java calls.

Add a keyword-only per-call options parameter to nltk.internals.java() and pass wrapper java_options directly to each subprocess invocation. Clean wrapper temporary input files from finally blocks so exception paths remove plaintext input.

Reported by KKfine via huntr. CVE-2026-12615 assigned.

CVE-2026-12614.8493007b3ec04bfa132ed5ca9cbecf127ecc9eda:
fix(security): avoid MaltParser process-wide CWD changes (#3682)

MaltParser.parse_tagged_sents() changed the process CWD to the model directory before invoking the external parser and restored it only after _execute() returned. Because os.chdir() is process-wide, concurrent relative-path I/O in the same process could be redirected into the model directory, and exceptions could leave the process CWD polluted.

Run the MaltParser subprocess with cwd set to the model directory instead of changing the Python process CWD. Also clean parser temp files from a finally block so they are removed on exception paths.

Reported by KKfine via huntr. CVE-2026-12614 assigned.

CVE-2026-12929.0624fecd45e48337a1f070856bdbcb10643e48c2:
fix(security): make METEOR word matching linear to stop quadratic-time DoS (CVE-2026-12929) (#3666)

* fix(security): make METEOR word matching linear to stop quadratic-time DoS (CVE-2026-12929)

nltk.translate.meteor_score's matcher (_match_enums, reached from the public
single_meteor_score/meteor_score) compares every hypothesis token against every
reference token, only short-circuiting on a match. For disjoint text no match
fires, so it runs the full O(len_hyp * len_ref); two further leftover stages
(_enum_stem_match -> _match_enums, and _enum_wordnetsyn_match's own nested scan)
re-run the same full scan, making a single scoring call quadratic in length
(CWE-770).

Replace the nested scans with a hash index from reference word to its positions:
each hypothesis word pops the highest available position of the same word, which
exactly mirrors the original reverse j-scan (latest still-unused reference word).
_enum_wordnetsyn_match takes the highest available position among a word's
synonyms. _match_enums is now O(len_hyp + len_ref) and the wordnet stage is
O(len_hyp * synonyms + len_ref); _enum_stem_match delegates to _match_enums so it
is fixed too. _enum_align_words already re-sorts matches by hypothesis index
before chunk counting, so only the matched-pair set and leftovers affect the
score -- both preserved.

Scores are unchanged: the meteor_score.py doctest (0.6944, 0.0) and test_meteor.py
(0.9921875) pass, and the full single_meteor_score was differentially compared to
the original on 4000 random English-word pairs (all three stages firing) with 0
mismatches. Extends test_meteor.py with a preserved-values test and a spawned
linear-time guard (disjoint 32k tokens: ~49 s before, sub-second after).

* Address Copilot review on the METEOR DoS regression test

Report the spawned worker's status via a multiprocessing.Queue instead of
os._exit(0)/os._exit(3), so a worker exception is surfaced to the assertion
(actionable CI failures) and drop the now-unused os import.

CVE-2026-12928.70a8b0560e12a1d638d97dabdf3845e58c153259:
fix(security): bound NgramCounter distinct-ngram count to stop unbounded-memory DoS (CVE-2026-12928) (#3665)

* fix(security): bound NgramCounter distinct-ngram count to stop unbounded-memory DoS (CVE-2026-12928)

nltk.lm.NgramCounter stores every distinct ngram of every order in a nested dict
tree with no size bound, so training a language model on an attacker-controlled
corpus of distinct tokens via the documented pipeline (padded_everygram_pipeline
+ MLE.fit -> NgramCounter.update) allocates memory proportional to the distinct
ngrams (~order * tokens) with no cap, OOM-killing the worker (CWE-770). ~512
bytes per distinct ngram, scaling linearly without limit.

Bound the number of distinct ngrams stored -- the quantity that drives memory --
with a tunable MAX_NGRAMS (default 10,000,000, ~5 GB), raising ValueError once
exceeded. The cap counts distinct entries (via an O(1) membership check on new
ngrams), not tokens processed, so a large but repetitive corpus (few distinct
ngrams) is not falsely refused. update() is the single chokepoint all counting
flows through, so LanguageModel.fit is protected too. The default is generous
enough for NLTK's documented corpora (e.g. Brown at the usual orders) and is
tunable; the produced counts are unchanged.

Counts and doctests are unchanged (all nltk/test/unit/lm tests pass). Extends
test_counter.py with TestNgramCounterMemoryBound: behaviour preservation, refusal
of an oversized distinct corpus, bounding of the documented fit pipeline, and no
false cap on a large repetitive corpus.

* Address Copilot review on the NgramCounter memory bound

- update(): probe with .get() instead of self[order][context] so testing whether
  a (context, word) pair is new does not eagerly create empty nested defaultdict
  entries; the real entries are created only after the MAX_NGRAMS guard passes,
  so an ngram refused by the bound leaves no partial contexts/orders behind.
- _note_new_ngram(): check the bound before incrementing _distinct, so a refused
  ngram (which is never stored) does not inflate the distinct-ngram tracker.

CVE-2026-12926.12f7d0bd0cf70ecd1d42f6919ac4d7749cacd7b8:
fix(security): make jaro_similarity flagged-position lookup O(1) to stop cubic DoS (CVE-2026-12926) (#3664)

* fix(security): make jaro_similarity flagged-position lookup O(1) to stop cubic DoS (CVE-2026-12926)

nltk.metrics.distance.jaro_similarity matches characters within an O(n**2)
window double loop and, inside it, tests `j not in flagged_2` against a list.
That membership test is O(len(flagged_2)), and on near-matching strings
flagged_2 grows toward n, adding a third linear factor -> O(n**3). A pair of
small near-identical strings then pins a CPU core for tens of seconds, and
jaro_winkler_similarity inherits it (CWE-770).

Store the flagged s2 positions in a set so the membership test is O(1),
restoring the algorithm's natural O(n**2) complexity. The guard already prevents
duplicates, so the set holds the same positions as the old list; sorting it into
a list for the transposition pass yields the same matches, transpositions and
score -- verified by differential testing the set-based vs list-based
implementation on 200k random pairs (identical float every time) and by
metrics.doctest / test_distance.py matching develop.

Extends nltk/test/unit/test_distance.py with a test asserting a near-matching
pair computes in quadratic (not cubic) time, run in a spawned process with a hard
timeout so a regression to the list membership cannot hang the suite (CPU-only,
no OOM risk).

* Address Copilot review on the jaro_similarity DoS fix

- Report the jaro test worker's status via a multiprocessing.Queue instead of
  os._exit(0), so any worker exception is surfaced to the assertion (drops the
  now-unused os import), matching the other DoS regression tests.
- Keep the matched s2 positions as a set (O(1) membership) and the sorted list
  used for the transposition pass as separate variables (matched_2 / flagged_2)
  rather than mutating one variable's type.

CVE-2026-12870.235853c21c0b7f35e79d71877ad587837f17ba6d:
fix(security): bound phrase_extraction default max_phrase_length to stop cubic DoS (CVE-2026-12870) (#3657)

* fix(security): bound phrase_extraction default max_phrase_length to stop cubic DoS (CVE-2026-12870)

nltk.translate.phrase_based.phrase_extraction defaults max_phrase_length to the
full sentence length (max_phrase_length or max(srclen, trglen)), so the default
path enumerates O(n**2) phrase pairs, each holding an O(n)-word string -- O(n**3)
total work and memory. A few-hundred-word sentence pair pins the CPU for
seconds-to-minutes and allocates hundreds of MB to GB (CWE-770); all three
arguments are untrusted and no non-default configuration is required.

Cap the defaulted max_phrase_length with MAX_PHRASE_EXTRACTION_DEFAULT_LEN (256):
when the sentinel would expand beyond it, raise ValueError asking for an explicit
max_phrase_length (e.g. 7, the usual phrase-based MT limit) instead of running
the O(n**3) path. An explicitly supplied max_phrase_length -- an informed choice
-- is never capped, so no caller that passes a length changes behaviour; the cap
is non-silent (raises rather than truncating) and tunable via the module
constant. The "not max_phrase_length" check preserves the original or-based
default selection exactly.

The documented 24-phrase example is unchanged (its default expands to 10 <= 256).
Adds nltk/test/unit/translate/test_phrase_based_security.py, which preserves that
example and the explicit-length behaviour and asserts the default over a long
pair is refused, run in a spawned process with a hard timeout (exit-code IPC) so
a regression cannot hang the suite.

* test: make phrase_extraction cap-boundary test cheap (review feedback)

test_default_allowed_up_to_the_cap called phrase_extraction at the cap with a
diagonal alignment, which forced the test to run the near-cubic enumeration and
build ~33k long phrase strings (~36 MB, ~0.5 s) -- slow and potentially flaky on
constrained CI runners. The default-length guard depends only on the sentence
length, not the alignment, so the boundary (no ValueError at exactly the cap) can
be checked with an empty alignment: the guard still runs on the full default
length but no phrases are built (~0.03 MB, ~12 ms). Result is now an empty set.

CVE-2026-12864.b6d75db532cb4f9383091a329fd8d9270aaac093:
fix(security): bound generate() derivation-expansion steps to stop unbounded-enumeration DoS (CVE-2026-12864) (#3654)

* fix(security): bound generate() derivation-expansion steps to stop unbounded-enumeration DoS (CWE-400)

nltk.parse.generate.generate uses a large default depth (recursionlimit//3,
~330) and no default cap on the number of sentences, so a tiny recursive
grammar derives an exponential (doubly-exponential for a self-embedding rule)
number of sentences. A 15-byte grammar like "S -> S S | 'a'" makes
generate(grammar) hang producing even the first sentence, or exhaust memory
when materialized (CWE-400). The grammar is untrusted input.

generate() now meters work with a shared _GenerationBudget: _generate_one
spends one unit per expansion, and once MAX_GENERATE_OPERATIONS (default
1_000_000) is exceeded it raises ValueError instead of running unbounded. The
budget is shared across the whole enumeration, so it bounds total work whether
the caller pulls one item or lists them all; it raises (rather than silently
truncating) so a capped run can't be mistaken for a complete one; and
MAX_GENERATE_OPERATIONS is tunable for larger terminating grammars.

Every terminating call is unaffected (the demo grammar's full enumeration costs
277 steps); generate.doctest and grammar.doctest pass unchanged. Adds
nltk/test/unit/test_generate.py, which preserves the doctest counts and asserts
the default-depth recursive grammar is refused, run in a spawned process with a
hard timeout so a regression cannot hang/OOM the suite.

* Address review feedback on generate() DoS-budget PR

Two points raised in review:

1. generate() used `if n:` to decide whether to cap the output, which treats
   n=0 as "no limit" and returns the full generator -- surprising given n is
   documented as "the maximum number of sentences to return". Use
   `if n is not None:` so n=0 honestly returns no sentences (and, for a
   recursive grammar, enumerates nothing rather than running to the budget
   limit). Adds a test for n=0 on both a finite and a recursive grammar.

2. The `:raise ValueError:` docstring used trailing-backslash line
   continuations, which collapsed the closing ``MAX_GENERATE_OPERATIONS``
   marker straight into the next word (broken RST inline-literal) and was
   inconsistent with NLTK's indented-continuation style. Rewrite it as indented
   continuation lines so it renders correctly.

generate.doctest, grammar.doctest and the unit tests pass unchanged.

CVE-2026-12261.7a5740af89feeb739193db766e11e85dfe78339c:
fix: enforce package ownership during ZIP extraction (#3625)

* fix: enforce package ownership during ZIP extraction (CVE-2026-12261)

Cross-package resource and model poisoning was possible because:

1. _unzip_iter extracted into a shared subdir namespace, allowing
   a package with subdir='taggers' to overwrite files belonging to
   any other package in that namespace without path traversal.

2. Integrity (size + sha256) was validated by _pkg_status() after
   the archive was already committed and extracted, so poisoned
   assets became live before any failure was surfaced.

Fix:
- Add expected_root parameter to _unzip_iter(). Both validation
  phases now reject any member whose top-level path component
  does not match the owning package id. Cross-package writes are
  blocked with a clear error message before any extraction occurs.
- Validate size and sha256_checksum on the .tmp file before
  os.replace(), failing closed and removing the temp file on
  any mismatch.
- Filesystem layout (zipdir = download_dir/subdir/) is preserved
  so _pkg_status() and NLTK data loaders see no change.

* fix: validate legacy MD5 checksums before extraction

CVE-2026-12919.4085d53c7793d3d6622f2bf02272faf54d4c3975:
fix(security): make feature-structure rename regex linear to stop quadratic ReDoS (CVE-2026-12919) (#3663)

* fix(security): make feature-structure rename regex linear to stop quadratic ReDoS (CVE-2026-12919)

nltk.featstruct._rename_variable strips a trailing run of digits from a variable
name with re.sub(r"\d+$", "", var.name). The greedy \d+ made a name with a long
run of digits not at the end (e.g. x000...0z) re-scan the run from every position
(match \d+, miss $, backtrack), which is quadratic in the run length -- so
renaming, or unifying (which renames by default), an untrusted feature structure
via the public FeatStruct.fromstring / rename_variables / unify pins a CPU core
(CWE-1333).

Add a (?<!\d) lookbehind so the greedy \d+ can start only at the beginning of a
run; interior positions then fail in O(1) instead of re-scanning, making the
substitution linear. The lookbehind only restricts where the run may start to
its natural boundary, so the stripped result is unchanged -- verified by
differential fuzzing the new vs old pattern on 300k random names (0 mismatches)
and by featstruct.doctest (335 attempted, 0 failed, matching develop). It is a
fixed-width lookbehind, supported on all tested Python versions (3.10+).

Adds nltk/test/unit/test_featstruct_redos.py, which preserves the trailing-digit
stripping and rename/unify behaviour and asserts a long digit-run name renames in
linear time, run in a spawned process with a hard timeout so a regression to the
quadratic pattern cannot hang the suite (it is CPU-only, no OOM risk).

* test: fail the featstruct ReDoS guard if the worker raises (review feedback)

The worker swallowed exceptions and always exited 0, so the ReDoS regression test
could pass without exercising the rename path (e.g. if parsing of the crafted
variable broke before rename_variables ran). The crafted feature structure is
valid and renames successfully, so any exception is unexpected: exit 0 only on a
completed rename and exit non-zero otherwise, so the parent assertion fails. The
hang case is still caught by the timeout.

CVE-2026-12890.7130b49223947fb787047261e128c0ce24ffc434:
fix(security): make valuation separator regex linear to stop quadratic ReDoS (CVE-2026-12890) (#3662)

nltk.sem.evaluate splits each valuation line on _VAL_SPLIT_RE = \s*=+>\s*. The
greedy =+ run made splitting a line that holds a long run of '=' not terminated
by '>' re-scan the run from every position (match =+, miss >, backtrack), which
is quadratic in the run length -- so a single untrusted valuation string passed
to the public Valuation.fromstring / read_valuation pins a CPU core (CWE-1333).

Add a (?<!=) lookbehind so the greedy =+ can start only at the beginning of a
run; interior positions then fail in O(1) instead of re-scanning, making the
split linear. The lookbehind only restricts where a match may start to the run
boundary the leftmost match already uses, so the split result is unchanged --
verified by differential fuzzing the new vs old pattern on 300k random strings
(0 mismatches) and by semantics.doctest matching develop (149 attempted, 20
pre-existing missing-corpus failures). It is a fixed-width lookbehind, supported
on all tested Python versions (3.10+).

Adds nltk/test/unit/test_valuation_redos.py, which preserves the parsed values
(including a multi-'=' separator) and asserts a long '=' run parses in linear
time, run in a spawned process with a hard timeout so a regression to the
quadratic pattern cannot hang the suite (it is CPU-only, no OOM risk).

CVE-2026-12886.2a42d9cabc98ef1b7e83e69812d2c0ab7e95e0f5:
fix(security): bound chart parse-tree extraction to stop exponential DoS (CVE-2026-12886) (#3661)

* fix(security): bound chart parse-tree extraction to stop exponential DoS (CVE-2026-12886)

nltk.parse.chart.ChartParser and subclasses build the chart in polynomial time
but Chart._trees materialises every parse tree eagerly into a list. With a tiny
highly-ambiguous grammar (e.g. the 15-byte S -> S S | 'a') the number of parses
is the Catalan number -- exponential in the sentence length -- so a short
sentence makes extraction hang or exhaust memory, and even obtaining the first
parse never returns (CWE-770). Both the grammar and the sentence are untrusted.

The parse count is inherently exponential, so it cannot be made polynomial
without changing semantics. Instead, meter every parse-tree node built with a
shared _ParseTreeBudget and raise ValueError once MAX_PARSE_TREES (1_000_000) is
exceeded. Chart.trees creates the budget and threads it through the recursive
Chart._trees, so the single chokepoint covers every chart parser
(ChartParser/BottomUp/TopDown/FeatureChartParser/Earley/probabilistic, which all
extract via chart.parses -> trees -> _trees). The budget is shared across the
recursion (including memoised reuse); it raises rather than silently truncating
the forest; and budget is an optional last param of the internal _trees, so the
public trees/parses signatures are unchanged. At the cap the worst case is
~0.4 s / ~280 MB, far beyond any realistic parse forest, and MAX_PARSE_TREES is
tunable.

Ordinary parses are unchanged (a PP-attachment sentence still yields 2 parses;
small Catalan forests are produced in full); parse.doctest and featgram.doctest
match develop. Adds nltk/test/unit/test_chart_parser.py, which preserves the
parses, refuses an over-cap forest (monkeypatched low cap, in process), and
asserts an exponential forest is refused not built, run in a spawned process
with a hard timeout so a regression cannot hang the suite.

* fix: thread parse-tree budget through CCGChart._trees; count partial-tree nodes

Address review feedback on the chart parse-tree budget:

1. Chart.trees() now calls self._trees(..., budget=budget), which broke the
   CCGChart._trees override (no budget parameter) -- CCGChartParser.parse() then
   raised "CCGChart._trees() got an unexpected keyword argument 'budget'" as soon
   as it produced a parse (confirmed). Add budget to the CCG override, thread it
   through the recursive calls, and spend on each constructed node so CCG charts
   are bounded by MAX_PARSE_TREES too. (CI missed this because no test reaches a
   complete CCG parse; ccg.doctest / ccg_semantics.doctest still pass, matching
   develop.)

2. The childless tree_class(elt, []) nodes built for incomplete edges (the
   complete=False / partial-tree path) were not counted, making MAX_PARSE_TREES
   an inaccurate node-construction bound. Spend the budget for those too.

CVE-2026-12873.26ddcd0e3a3c04441fafacc16c7354038b744aa1:
fix(security): bound DRT resolve_anaphora work to stop quadratic time+memory DoS (CVE-2026-12873) (#3660)

* fix(security): bound DRT resolve_anaphora work to stop quadratic time+memory DoS (CVE-2026-12873)

nltk.sem.drt.resolve_anaphora resolves each PRO(x) condition by scanning every
discourse referent on the trail and retaining the compatible ones as a candidate
list kept in the result, so a DRS with N referents and N pronouns performs
O(N**2) examinations and retains O(N**2) candidates -- quadratic time and
resident memory. A small crafted DRS string via the public
DrtExpression.fromstring(...).resolve_anaphora() then pins the CPU and exhausts
memory (CWE-770).

The O(N**2) is partly the result size (each pronoun genuinely resolves to its
list of antecedents), so it cannot be made O(N) without changing semantics.
Instead, meter every (pronoun, referent) examination with a shared budget
threaded through the recursion and raise AnaphoraResolutionException once
MAX_ANAPHORA_OPERATIONS (1_000_000) is exceeded. Retained candidates <=
examinations, so this bounds both the time and memory channels. The budget is an
optional last parameter (default None), so existing callers are unchanged; it
raises the existing domain exception (already caught by
inference.discourse.process_thread) rather than silently truncating; and the
constant is tunable. At the cap the worst case is ~0.5 s / ~70 MB, while 1e6
examinations is ~1000x any real discourse.

The resolve_anaphora doctests are unchanged. Adds nltk/test/unit/test_drt_anaphora.py,
which preserves the documented outputs and asserts an oversized DRS is refused;
that check is bounded by the budget (~70 MB) and safe even if the guard were
removed, so it catches a regression without hanging/OOM-ing the suite.

* test: use f-strings in DRT anaphora test to satisfy pyupgrade

The pre-commit pyupgrade hook (--py310-plus) rewrites "%s"-tuple formatting to
.format(); the _flat_drs helper used "([%s],[%s])" % (refs, conds), which failed
the hook. Use f-strings throughout the helper instead -- pyupgrade's target form,
which it leaves unchanged -- so pre-commit passes.

* Address review feedback on DRT anaphora budget PR

Three points raised in review:

1 & 2. test_oversized_discourse_is_refused drove the real 1,000,000-step budget
   in process, making the test slow and memory-heavy. Monkeypatch
   nltk.sem.drt.MAX_ANAPHORA_OPERATIONS down to a small cap and size the DRS with
   math.isqrt (a DRS with n referents and n pronouns does n**2 examinations, so
   n = isqrt(cap) + 1 exceeds it). The guard now trips at ~the small cap's worth
   of candidates, so the test is fast and low-memory while still regression-safe
   (without the guard this n completes without raising, so the missing exception
   is detected).

3. _AnaphoraBudget read its limit from the public, overridable
   MAX_ANAPHORA_OPERATIONS global. Validate it is a positive int in __init__ so a
   bad override fails immediately with a clear ValueError rather than an obscure
   error mid-resolution.

drt.py doctest and the regression tests pass; behaviour on valid input is
unchanged.

CVE-2026-12871.583d63ac3ded20a70e073b2bcd1dc60304070903:
fix(security): route data.retrieve write through the pathsec sandbox (CVE-2026-12871) (#3659)

* fix(security): route data.retrieve write through the pathsec sandbox (CVE-2026-12871)

nltk.data.retrieve copied a resource to a caller-supplied filename using the
builtin open(filename, "wb"), bypassing NLTK's centralized file-access sentinel
(nltk.pathsec). With the sandbox enabled (pathsec.ENFORCE, on by default) and an
attacker-influenced filename, this wrote arbitrary local files outside the
allowed data roots; since the attacker controls both the destination and the
content, a shell-init/login-profile/authorized_keys/autostart target escalates
to code execution as the victim (CWE-22). The read side (_open) was already
guarded; only the write target bypassed pathsec.

Write through pathsec.open (already imported as _secure_open and used elsewhere
in data.py), which runs validate_path (allowed data roots + symlink resolution)
before delegating to the builtin open. When the sandbox is disabled pathsec.open
delegates straight to open, so behaviour is unchanged; when enabled, an in-root
target still writes while an out-of-root target is rejected before any bytes are
written.

Extends nltk/test/unit/test_data_security.py: with the allowed roots monkeypatched
to a temp dir, an out-of-root target is rejected (and nothing written) while an
in-root target still copies the bytes, plus that behaviour is unchanged when the
sandbox is off. The data.doctest retrieve examples write under tempfile.gettempdir()
(an allowed root) and are unaffected.

* test: build retrieve() file URLs with Path.as_uri() for portability (review feedback)

The retrieve() sandbox tests built the source file URL via "file://" + str(src),
which is not portable (Windows paths, spaces, characters needing URL-escaping).

CVE-2026-12868.c65ca13e873721c5abf5a4ce8c78510c5956d839:
fix(security): make Cistem stemmer linear to stop quadratic-time DoS (CVE-2026-12868) (#3658)

* fix(security): make Cistem stemmer linear to stop quadratic-time DoS (CVE-2026-12868)

Cistem._segment_inner stripped 1-2 trailing characters per iteration with
regex.subn("", word), which rebuilds the whole remaining string on every
removal. With ~n iterations (a word of repeated strippable suffixes) and O(n)
work per iteration, stemming is O(n**2) in the word length, so a single ~60 KB
token pins a CPU core for ~15 s (CWE-770). The input is one untrusted string and
no non-default configuration is required.

All four patterns (e[mr]$, nd$, t$, [esn]$) are anchored at the end and remove
only 1-2 characters there, so strip characters off the end of a list in O(1) per
step and join once, making the method O(n). Python's $ matches at the end or
just before a single trailing newline, so such a newline is transparent to the
patterns and must be preserved; the loop reproduces that exactly (handling it in
the same O(n) path, so a newline-laced word cannot re-trigger the quadratic
behaviour). The four now-unused compiled regexes are removed.

Behaviour is unchanged: the doctest stem/segment examples pass in both case
modes, and the new loop was differentially fuzzed against the original on 300k
random words (including the replace_to special chars, German chars, capitals and
embedded/trailing newlines) with zero mismatches. Adds nltk/test/unit/test_cistem.py,
which preserves the documented outputs and asserts a long word stems in linear
time, run in a spawned process with a hard timeout so a regression cannot hang
the suite.

* docs: name the stdlib re engine in the Cistem ReDoS notes (review feedback)

The fix comment and the test docstring said "regex.subn", which reads like the
third-party ``regex`` module; the original code called ``Pattern.subn`` on
compiled stdlib ``re`` patterns. Reword to "the compiled re patterns'
Pattern.subn" so the security note is unambiguous. Comment/docstring only -- no
behaviour change.

CVE-2026-12867.8527d08138ae674f33f7fb08b2f8b55c3cf11861:
fix(security): route DependencyGraph.load through the pathsec sandbox (CVE-2026-12867) (#3656)

* fix(security): route DependencyGraph.load through the pathsec sandbox (CVE-2026-12867)

nltk.parse.dependencygraph.DependencyGraph.load opened the caller-supplied
filename with the builtin open, bypassing NLTK's centralized file-access
sentinel (nltk.pathsec). Where an application enables the sandbox as a boundary
(pathsec.ENFORCE, on by default) and feeds load an attacker-influenced filename,
this allowed arbitrary local files to be read and their parsed content returned
via the graph's node words (CWE-22).

Read through pathsec.open instead, as the other file-reading entry points in the
tree already do; it runs validate_path (allowed data roots + symlink resolution)
before delegating to the builtin open. When the sandbox is disabled, pathsec.open
delegates straight to open, so behaviour is unchanged; when enabled, an in-root
file still loads while an out-of-root path is rejected.

Adds nltk/test/unit/test_dependencygraph_security.py, which monkeypatches the
allowed roots to a temp dir and asserts an out-of-root path is rejected while an
in-root file still loads, plus that behaviour is unchanged when the sandbox is
off.

* Tighten DependencyGraph.load sandbox regression tests (review feedback)

Two points raised in review:

1. The out-of-root case asserted pytest.raises((PermissionError, ValueError)).
   The global sandbox (no required_root) only ever raises PermissionError for
   an unauthorized path (ValueError is reserved for the scoped required_root
   path, which pathsec.open does not use), so accepting ValueError made the test
   lax and could mask an unrelated failure. Assert PermissionError exactly.

2. test_load_unchanged_when_sandbox_disabled wrote into tmp_path, which is
   normally inside tempfile.gettempdir() and therefore already an allowed root,
   so it did not actually exercise reading an out-of-root path with the sandbox
   off. Force _get_allowed_roots to return an empty set so the file is
   unambiguously out-of-root, and assert that with ENFORCE off the load emits
   the expected RuntimeWarning but still reads the file.

Both tests pass; the fix itself is unchanged.

CVE-2026-12861.3e9d537ac5ce698a98148398cd4c5e8da59d9965:
fix(security): bound everygrams default max_len to stop unbounded-allocation DoS (CVE-2026-12861) (#3655)

* fix(security): bound everygrams default max_len to stop unbounded-allocation DoS (CVE-2026-12861)

nltk.util.everygrams defaults max_len to a -1 sentinel that expands to the full
sequence length, so calling it with default arguments enumerates every n-gram
of every length up to the input length over each window: O(n**2) tuples of
average length O(n), i.e. O(n**3) total size. Materializing the result over a
few-thousand-token sequence allocates many gigabytes and OOM-kills the worker
(CWE-770). The sequence is untrusted input and no non-default configuration is
required.

Every legitimate caller passes an explicit, small max_len (which keeps the
output linear); only the default path is unbounded. The defaulted max_len is
now capped by MAX_EVERYGRAMS_DEFAULT_LEN (256): when the sentinel would expand
beyond it, everygrams raises ValueError asking for an explicit max_len instead
of allocating O(n**3). An explicitly supplied max_len -- an informed choice --
is never capped, so no existing caller changes behaviour; the cap is non-silent
(raises rather than truncating) and tunable via the module constant.

The docstring examples, test_util.py (including the default-max_len
test_everygrams_without_padding), and the lm tests/doctest are unaffected. Adds
nltk/test/unit/test_everygrams_alloc.py, which preserves those outputs and
asserts the default over a long sequence is refused, run in a spawned process
(address-space limit where supported, plus a hard timeout) so a regression
cannot OOM/hang the suite.

* test: make everygrams DoS guard robust on free-threaded Python (3.14t)

The spawned-process guard reported its result through a multiprocessing.Queue
and set an RLIMIT_AS address-space cap. On free-threaded Python 3.14t that cap
prevented the Queue's feeder thread from starting ("can't start new thread"), so
the worker's result never reached the parent and the test failed even though the
fix worked (the worker did raise the expected ValueError).

Drop the RLIMIT_AS cap and the queue; the worker now reports its outcome via its
exit code (0 = refused as expected, non-zero = materialized/other). No queue or
feeder thread is involved, so it is robust on free-threaded builds, and the hard
timeout still bounds a regression.

* Address review feedback on everygrams default-max_len cap PR

Two points raised in review:

1. The everygrams `:raise ValueError:` docstring used literal trailing
   backslashes at line ends, which render as escaping artifacts in the built
   docs. Reformat it as an indented continuation paragraph (no backslashes).

2. The allocation regression test's worker called list(everygrams(toks)); if a
   regression removed the guard, that would materialize the full O(n**3) result
   (~10 GB at n=2000) and could trip the OS OOM killer, destabilizing the whole
   CI job rather than failing one test. Consume the iterator without
   materializing it (`for _ in everygrams(toks): pass`): each tuple is transient
   so peak memory stays flat (measured ~0 MB vs ~2.3 GB for list() at n=1200),
   and a regression is caught by the parent's timeout instead of an OOM. Rename
   the now-inaccurate _EXIT_MATERIALIZED outcome to _EXIT_ENUMERATED.

util.py doctest and the regression tests pass unchanged.

CVE-2026-12840.e7668b593fba1eeb5197987ebbb3251302bc678b:
fix(security): bound Model.satisfy quantifier-nesting cost to stop combinatorial DoS (CVE-2026-12840) (#3653)

* fix(security): bound Model.satisfy quantifier-nesting cost to stop combinatorial DoS (CVE-2026-12840)

Model.satisfy iterates the entire domain once per nested quantifier/lambda,
so a formula with k nested binders costs O(|domain| ** k). k comes entirely
from the untrusted formula string, so a tiny formula (e.g. nine nested
"all" quantifiers with a "(x0 = x0)" body) drives an unbounded amount of
computation and wedges the worker (CWE-770).

satisfy is now a thin wrapper that refuses a formula up front when its
worst-case cost |domain| ** max-binder-depth would exceed
Model.MAX_SATISFY_OPERATIONS (default 1_000_000); the original recursion is
preserved verbatim as _satisfy. The depth is computed in time linear in the
formula size without running it, and the cost check multiplies incrementally
and bails on the first overflow, so it never builds a large integer even for
an absurd nesting depth.

Adds nltk/test/unit/test_sem_evaluate.py: unit-tests the depth helper,
confirms legitimate formulas still evaluate, and asserts a deeply-nested
formula is refused (run in a spawned process with a hard timeout so a
regression cannot hang the suite).

* docs: clarify what Model.satisfy's cost guard actually bounds

Address review feedback: the MAX_SATISFY_OPERATIONS comment/docstrings
described the limit as an upper bound on the *total* domain-iteration steps a
satisfy call may take, but the check only bounds |domain| ** max_binder_depth
-- the worst-case domain-value combinations along the most deeply nested
quantifier/lambda path. For a formula with independent sibling quantifiers
(e.g. "(all x.P(x)) & (all y.Q(y))") the true total is the sum of the branches,
which the max-based depth undercounts, so the documented guarantee was
inaccurate.

Reword the comment, docstrings and error message to state precisely what is
bounded: the combinatorial nesting factor |domain| ** (nesting depth), which is
the term that actually blows up. Sibling quantifiers only add a factor linear
in the formula's size (they do not multiply), so a small formula still cannot
amplify into super-linear work -- the security property is unchanged. This is a
documentation-only change; the guard logic and all behaviour are identical
(evaluate.py doctest and the unit tests pass unchanged).

CVE-2026-12839.b6155c03362fe003ecbf7e383180b9e06f42ae7e:
fix(security): sparse ConfusionMatrix to stop quadratic-memory DoS (CVE-2026-12839) (#3652)

* fix(security): sparse ConfusionMatrix to stop quadratic-memory DoS (CVE-2026-12839)

ConfusionMatrix built and retained a dense V x V list-of-lists, where V is the
number of distinct values across reference + test. Since the allocation is sized
by the distinct-value count (not the item count or byte length), a short
all-distinct input forces a V x V matrix: a few thousand distinct labels cost
hundreds of MB and ~20000 reach multiple GB, OOM-killing the worker
(CWE-770; CVE-2026-12839).

Store the matrix sparsely as a dict mapping each observed (reference index,
test index) pair to its count, so cost is proportional to the observed pairs
rather than V**2. All access points use non-creating .get so a read never
re-densifies: __getitem__ -> self._confusion.get((i, j), 0); pretty_format
renders cells via .get; the sort_by_count row totals in pretty_format/evaluate
use a _row_total(i) helper instead of sum(self._confusion[i]);
recall/precision/f_measure are unchanged (they go through __getitem__).
_max_conf/_total/_correct/_values/_indices keep the same values.

Behaviour preserved: metrics.doctest (the byte-exact matrix print-outs incl.
sort_by_count/truncate/values_in_chart) passes 85/0, the confusionmatrix.py
evaluate() doctest passes 9/9, and cm[i,j] (incl. absent pairs ->0) /
recall / precision / repr are unchanged.

Adds nltk/test/unit/test_confusionmatrix.py: sparse storage, preserved public
API, and an all-distinct allocation guard (peak memory bounded, run in a spawned
process with a hard timeout). The sparse and memory tests fail against the
pre-fix dense version (~210 MB at 5000 labels); 6000 labels drop from ~319 MB
to ~0.9 MB.

* perf: cache ConfusionMatrix row totals so sort_by_count stays linear

Addresses review feedback: _row_total recomputed a row total by scanning the
whole sparse map on every call, and sort_by_count calls it once per label, so
ordering was O(V * nnz) -- quadratic again for a large all-distinct input (even
when truncate keeps the output small), reintroducing a CPU-time DoS in the very
path this PR hardens.

Accumulate per-reference-row totals in the existing single construction loop
(zero extra passes; the row total for reference index i is just the number of
items whose reference is value i) and have _row_total read from that cache, so
each lookup is O(1) and the whole sort is O(V log V + nnz). Row totals are
identical to the previous full-scan values; metrics.doctest (incl. the
byte-exact sort_by_count output) and the confusionmatrix doctest/unit tests are
unchanged. Measured sort cost on an all-distinct input drops from 675 ms to
0.3 ms at 8000 labels (and the gap widens quadratically with size).

CVE-2026-12837.f455b85a5183a54c30e667aaf1254331a93c6fa7:
fix(security): sparse Alignment index to stop unbounded-allocation DoS (CVE-2026-12837) (#3651)

* fix(security): sparse Alignment index to stop unbounded-allocation DoS (CVE-2026-12837)

Alignment parses GIZA word-alignment strings; each pair's left index is an
unbounded int() and the largest left index is stored as self._len. _build_index
then allocated a dense list [[] for _ in range(self._len + 1)] -- one list per
left index -- so a single tiny pair with a huge left index (e.g.
"0-0 100000000-1") forced a multi-GB allocation on the first __getitem__/range(),
OOM-killing the worker. Amplification is tens of millions x the input size; no
auth or non-default config required (CWE-770; CVE-2026-12837).

Make the index sparse: a dict keyed only by the left indices that occur, so its
size is bounded by the number of pairs rather than the (attacker-controlled)
largest index. __getitem__ returns self._index.get(key, []) and range() iterates
the occurring keys instead of range(self._len + 1); the cache check is
``self._index is None`` so an empty alignment still builds its index once.
self._len is still computed (O(pairs), just an int) for backward compatibility.

Behaviour preserved for all documented/used access (a[i] -> list of pairs,
range() -> sorted right indices, invert/issubset/==); a[i] now returns [] for an
absent left index instead of IndexError beyond _len, and index slicing is no
longer supported (it would reintroduce the O(largest-index) allocation; nothing
in-tree uses it).

Adds nltk/test/unit/translate/test_alignment.py: sparse-index, preserved
__getitem__/range/invert behaviour, and a huge-left-index allocation guard run in
a spawned process with a hard timeout. The sparse and allocation tests fail
against the pre-fix dense version; Alignment doctests and translate unit tests
pass.

* Address review feedback on Alignment sparse-index PR

Two points raised in review:

1. Alignment.__getitem__ used dict.get, which silently accepted slices and
   other non-integer keys (e.g. a[0:2] or a['0']) and returned [], masking
   caller bugs. Reject non-integer keys with TypeError now; the sparse index
   has no contiguous range to slice, so such a lookup should fail loudly.
   Integer indices behave as before (an absent left index still returns []).

2. The allocation regression test used _HUGE = 100_000_000; if a dense-index
   regression were reintroduced, that list would be ~6 GB and could OOM the CI
   host (even in the child process) instead of failing cleanly. Lower it to
   2_000_000: the dense form would still be unmistakable (the index would hold
   _HUGE + 1 keys instead of 2, caught by the key-count assertion) but is only
   ~128 MB, so it can't OOM the host.

Adds a test that non-integer keys raise TypeError. The Alignment doctests and
the existing sparse/range tests are unchanged.

CVE-2026-12178.3da396507c39040db8f76f3c0a30c397ebed622c:
fix(security): stop symlink-following deletion in downloader stale-cleanup (CWE-59) (#3643)

Sibling of the downloader arbitrary-write finding (CVE-2026-12178, lexical
containment check): same root cause (the check does not resolve symlinks),
different sink. When a package is STALE, _download_package cleans up the
prior unzip directory with _safe_rmtree(unzipdir). unzipdir is filepath with
".zip" removed -- lexically inside download_dir, so never separately
validated or symlink-resolved. _safe_rmtree walks it with
os.walk(topdown=False), and os.walk follows a symlinked TOP (followlinks
only governs subdirs). So a pre-existing symlink at unzipdir pointing
outside download_dir causes recursive deletion of the link's TARGET --
arbitrary file/directory deletion. STALE is reached by planting a wrong-size
X.zip plus a symlink X -> victim in a shared download dir; the victim
running the normal nltk.download('X') then deletes the target.

Make _safe_rmtree never follow a symlink: if the top is a symlink, remove
the link itself (os.remove deletes the link, not its target) and return;
also handle symlinked subdirs (which os.walk lists but does not descend) by
removing the link rather than failing rmdir on them. Real directories are
removed exactly as before.

Verified: the report PoC no longer deletes the victim (only the planted
symlink is removed); a real stale unzipdir with nested files is still fully
removed; test_downloader_atomic passes.

CVE-2026-0848.20400ae6ac462ef206d4fe3c5145f54c4e89bd54:
fix(security): do not run the candc/boxer binary from the CWD (CWE-426) (#3623)

Boxer resolved its candc/boxer executables with find_binary() and ran them via
subprocess.Popen. find_binary() also matches a binary relative to the current
working directory -- a relative bin_dir yields ./candc, and even the default
bin_dir=None matches a candc/candc directory in the CWD (find_file_iter joins
the name with itself). Such a result contains a separator, so Popen executes it
directly from the CWD (not $PATH), and the CWD match is tried before the CANDC
environment variable, so an attacker who can plant a candc/boxer file there gets
code execution -- an untrusted search path (CWE-426/CWE-427).

Resolve via find_binary_iter and use the first absolute candidate, skipping any
CWD-relative match; an absolute bin_dir, the CANDC environment variable and a
$PATH lookup are unchanged. Add regression tests. Same class as the MaltParser
(#3616), ReppTokenizer (#3618), Weka (#3620) and Senna (#3621) fixes and as
CVE-2026-0848.
CVE-2026-0848.5acf63c26e9eb31c6c42a38d2e6b1878fb5208a8:
fix(security): do not run the senna binary from the CWD (CWE-829) (#3621)

* fix(security): do not run the senna binary from the CWD (CWE-829)

Senna.__init__ accepted a relative senna_path (e.g. ".") and resolved the
executable against the current working directory. executable() returns a path
that contains a separator (e.g. ./senna-osx), and subprocess.Popen runs such a
path directly from the CWD without consulting $PATH, so an attacker who can
write a senna-<platform> file there had it executed -- arbitrary code execution
from an untrusted location (CWE-829), reachable via an untrusted search path
(CWE-426/CWE-427). Reached through SennaTagger / SennaChunkTagger /
SennaNERTagger, which all forward a directory to Senna.

Only resolve the executable against an explicit absolute senna_path; a relative
path falls through to the (also absolute) SENNA environment variable instead of
the CWD. Add regression tests. Same class as the MaltParser (#3616),
ReppTokenizer (#3618) and Weka (#3620) fixes and as CVE-2026-0848.

* fix(senna): fail fast in __init__ when no executable is found (review feedback)

When an absolute senna_path was given but the platform binary was missing and
SENNA was unset (or non-absolute), __init__ fell through without raising,
leaving an invalid _path and deferring the LookupError to tag_sents() -- despite
the comment saying the executable is verified in __init__. Resolve the path
(absolute senna_path, then absolute SENNA) and raise LookupError at the end if
the executable still is not found, so construction fails fast and consistently.
The security semantics are unchanged (relative senna_path / relative SENNA are
still rejected and the CWD is never used). Add a regression test.
CVE-2026-0848.880b6873aa70f67fc81e100085c8840e170c9e14:
fix(security): do not load weka.jar from the CWD (CWE-494) (#3620)

* fix(security): do not load weka.jar from the CWD (CWE-494)

config_weka() searched for weka.jar with the current working directory (".")
listed first in _weka_search, before the system locations and WEKAHOME. A
./weka.jar planted in the CWD by an attacker was therefore selected and executed
via java -cp ./weka.jar weka.classifiers.bayes.NaiveBayes ... -- loading and
running classes from an unverified jar with no integrity check (CWE-494),
reachable through an untrusted search path (CWE-426). config_weka() runs
automatically the first time a WekaClassifier classifies or trains, so simply
using a Weka classifier in such a directory triggers it.

Drop "." from _weka_search; WEKAHOME or an explicit config_weka(classpath=...)
must be used to point at a trusted weka.jar. Add regression tests. Same class as
the MaltParser (#3616) and ReppTokenizer (#3618) fixes and as CVE-2026-0848.

* test(weka): isolate search path in tests; copy _weka_search before insert (review feedback)

- Neutralise _weka_search in the autouse fixture so the regression test does
  not depend on a host-installed weka.jar (e.g. /usr/share/weka) on the runner,
  and add a direct assertion that the CWD is absent from the default search path.
- config_weka() now copies _weka_search before inserting WEKAHOME, so repeated
  calls no longer mutate the module-level default search order.

GHSA-RF74-V2FM-23PW.c1c1ee39b3c3541148b607ee85ae2745594a7a6b:
fix(security): bound LogicParser recursion depth to prevent uncaught RecursionError (CWE-674) (#3617)

* fix(security): bound LogicParser recursion depth to prevent uncaught RecursionError (CWE-674)

LogicParser is a recursive-descent parser: each nested sub-expression recurses
through process_next_expression. Deeply nested input (e.g.
Expression.fromstring("-" * 5000 + "p")) recursed until Python raised an uncaught
RecursionError, crashing the caller -- a denial of service from a few hundred
bytes of input (uncontrolled recursion). Same class as GHSA-rf74-v2fm-23pw, which
was fixed for the JSON decoder with a depth cap.

Cap the expression-nesting depth at LogicParser.MAX_PARSE_DEPTH (default 200, well
below the ~330 at which CPython's default recursion limit is reached) and raise a
normal LogicalExpressionException past it. Ordinary expressions are unaffected.
Add regression tests.

Reachable via the public Expression.fromstring / LogicParser().parse (and the
DrtParser subclass).

* fix(security): address review on the LogicParser recursion-depth guard

- raise the depth-limit LogicalExpressionException with a 1-based index
  (self._currentIndex + 1), consistent with ExpectedMoreTokensException; this
  avoids a secondary KeyError in parse()'s caret formatting (mapping[index - 1])
  when the limit is hit before any token is consumed (e.g. MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 0);
- drop the redundant second parse in the regression test (pytest.raises already
  fails on an unexpected RecursionError) and correct the wording (this is
  uncontrolled recursion, not ReDoS; nesting up to the cap parses, beyond raises).
GHSA-RF74-V2FM-23PW.00cdcd392142e6c745e7120c8d50a24127df5fad:
Fix GHSA-rf74-v2fm-23pw: unbounded recursion in JSONTaggedDecoder

JSONTaggedDecoder.decode_obj() recursed without depth limit,
allowing a crafted deeply-nested JSON payload to trigger
RecursionError and crash the process (denial of service).

Fix:
- Add MAX_DECODE_DEPTH = 200 class attribute as hard limit
- Add _depth counter parameter to decode_obj() that raises
  ValueError when exceeded
- Catch RecursionError in decode() for payloads that exceed
  Python's C-level json parser recursion limit (~1000) before
  decode_obj is reached

No other recursive JSON decoding paths exist in the codebase.
The stdlib json.load/json.loads calls in data.py, help.py,
sentiment/util.py, twitter/common.py, and tag/perceptron.py
do not use JSONTaggedDecoder and are not affected.

CVE-2021-3828.b02e9ee8da67004559f55547082f706d52087a85:
fix(security): prevent ReDoS in SensevalCorpusReader _fixXML (CWE-400) (#3614)

* fix(security): prevent ReDoS in SensevalCorpusReader _fixXML (CWE-1333)

_fixXML normalises Senseval pseudo-XML before parsing. Two of its substitutions
used plain re patterns whose lazy/greedy whitespace and token runs rescan a long
token / whitespace run that lacks the trailing <p="..."/> tag quadratically: a
crafted instance body such as "x" * 128000 hangs the reader (ReDoS). Same class
as CVE-2021-3828.

Compile both with the regex module (already a dependency) using possessive
quantifiers. The token class [^<>\s] cannot cross its surrounding separators and
\s cannot cross the literal '"', so the substitutions are match-for-match
identical (verified) while the scan becomes linear. Add regression tests.

Reachable via SensevalCorpusReader.instances() / .raw() (and
nltk.corpus.senseval) with the untrusted corpus file content as input.

* test(senseval): address review feedback on the ReDoS regression test

Test-only cleanup (the _fixXML fix is unchanged):

- drop the unused `os` import;
- correct the comments (the crafted token is ~128 KB, not ~256 KB);
- pass the fileid as a one-element list so CorpusReader treats it as an exact
  fileid rather than a regexp (where `.` would be a wildcard).
CVE-2021-3828.022fe14b8095ea91c1c653a0f8e1f4990ccfbc5f:
fix(security): prevent ReDoS in TextTilingTokenizer paragraph-break regex (CWE-1333) (#3612)

TextTilingTokenizer._mark_paragraph_breaks scans for blank-line paragraph
breaks with [ \t\r\f\v]*\n[ \t\r\f\v]*\n[ \t\r\f\v]*. With the plain greedy `re`
pattern, finditer rescans a long horizontal-whitespace run that has no blank
line quadratically: a crafted whitespace blob such as " \t" * 128000 hangs
tokenize() (ReDoS). Same class as CVE-2021-3828 / CVE-2021-43854.

Use possessive quantifiers (regex module, already a dependency) so each
whitespace run is non-backtracking. The whitespace class does not overlap "\n",
so the matches are unchanged (verified identical finditer output) while the
scan becomes linear. Add regression tests.

Reachable via the public TextTilingTokenizer().tokenize(text), where text is
untrusted input.
CVE-2021-3828.042359aa80c0428f59ff0f19a1c93e42a99686da:
fix(security): prevent ReDoS in ReviewsCorpusReader FEATURES regex (CWE-1333) (#3583)

* fix(security): bound ReviewsCorpusReader FEATURES label to prevent ReDoS (CWE-1333)

The FEATURES regex used an unbounded feature label ((?:(?:\w+\s)+)?\w+), so
re.findall rescans a long, bracket-less review line quadratically: a crafted
corpus line such as "word " * 100000 hangs the reader (ReDoS). Same class as
CVE-2021-3828.

Bound the label to a word plus up to 50 single-whitespace-separated words
(\w+(?:\s\w+){0,50}), making extraction linear. Real feature labels are short
noun phrases, so extraction on normal corpora is unchanged (verified identical
findall output). Add regression tests.

Reachable via nltk.corpus.product_reviews_1.reviews()/.features()/.sents().

* test(reviews): harden ReDoS regression tests per review

Addresses Copilot's review on #3583 (test-file feedback only; the FEATURES
regex fix is unchanged):

- Run the "must not hang" checks in a separate spawned process with a hard
  timeout and terminate() on overrun, instead of a daemon thread. A quadratic
  regression can no longer keep a runaway thread burning CPU for the rest of the
  suite, and the worker's exceptions are propagated back to the assertions
  rather than swallowed.
- Assert the end-to-end reader actually produced a result (one Review, no
  features) so a crash inside the worker can no longer masquerade as a pass.
- Use the tmp_path fixture instead of tempfile.mkdtemp(), so the temp corpus is
  cleaned up automatically.
- Drop the unused `re` import (ruff F401).

GHSA-R6GQ-WHWQ-MVG9.896a8ee981d8089b9edc2309aa10dcac6e2dec48:
Add realpath symlink check to FileSystemPathPointer.join()

After the existing lexical normpath check, resolve symlinks with
realpath() and verify the result stays within the corpus root.
This prevents symlink escapes where a path looks lexically
contained but resolves outside the root via a symlink.

Also blocks absolute file IDs.

Fixes GHSA-r6gq-whwq-mvg9. Does not touch open() — that is
handled by pathsec.open() via _secure_open.

GHSA-R6GQ-WHWQ-MVG9.cbe04c348677ee0d80dd4753d602d5915faad95f:
Unconditionally enforce path containment in FileSystemPathPointer

FileSystemPathPointer is the trust boundary for corpus readers.
Its open() and join() methods must always enforce containment
regardless of pathsec.ENFORCE setting.

Changes:
- Add _check_containment(): resolves symlinks with realpath() and
  verifies the path is within an allowed nltk.data.path directory.
  Always raises ValueError on violation (not warn-only).
- open(): calls _check_containment() before opening, fixing
  GHSA-72r2-7mfr-5xr9 (no-op sandbox check)
- join(): adds realpath-based symlink resolution check after the
  lexical normpath check, fixing GHSA-r6gq-whwq-mvg9 (symlink
  escape). Also blocks absolute file IDs.

These checks are independent of ENFORCE=True/False because they
protect the corpus reader sandbox, not general file I/O.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
